title: How to Run an Online Esports Tournament
description: Run an online esports tournament: choose a format, count matches, write rules, handle check-in and disputes, staff match day and plan the broadcast well.
intro: Running an online esports tournament means choosing a bracket format that fits your field size and schedule, writing rules that settle disputes before they start, and keeping a small team on hand to move matches along. The format sets how many matches you must schedule, the rules set how many arguments you must referee, and the tooling sets how much of this you do by hand. This playbook covers each of those in order, from the first format decision to the post-event wrap-up.
key_takeaways: Match count comes from the format: single elimination needs one fewer match than teams, a single round-robin needs every pair to meet once.
Double elimination takes one or two fewer than twice the number of teams in games, so 8 teams play 14 or 15.
Swiss pairing keeps everyone playing a fixed number of rounds without a full round-robin, but needs software to pair rounds.
Written rules for check-in, disconnects, results and disputes matter more than the bracket tool you choose.
Integrity provisions belong in your rules and participation terms, as bodies such as ESIC publish model clauses for exactly that.

sections.h2: Fix the constraints first: field size, time and staff
paras: Before choosing a format, write down three numbers: how many teams or players you expect, how many hours of match play you can host, and how many admins will be online. Everything else follows from them. A 64-player field with two admins and a Sunday afternoon cannot run a long group stage, whatever the format would look like on paper.

Also decide whether this is a one-off cup or the first event in a series. A series wants a ruleset that you can reuse, a results record, and a seeding method that can use earlier results. A one-off can stay simpler. Decide this now because it affects which tool you register on and which data you keep.

sections.h2: Choose a format and count the matches
paras: The four common formats each trade fairness against time. Wikipedia's pages on each describe how they work, and you can turn their definitions into a match count before you promise anyone a schedule.

In a single-elimination tournament the loser of each match is out immediately, and winners advance until a final. With a field of n teams, exactly n minus 1 matches are needed, since every match removes one team and one remains. It is the fastest format and the harshest, because one bad result ends a team's day.

A double-elimination tournament gives a team a second life: a participant is out only after losing two games or matches. Wikipedia notes that the number of games is one or two less than twice the number of teams, so 8 teams would see 14 or 15 games, and that fields of a power of two such as 8, 16 or 32 avoid byes. The extra match is the grand final reset, played only if the team coming from the lower bracket wins the first one.

In a round-robin each participant meets every other participant once, and a double round-robin has each pair meet twice. Match count is the number of pairs: n times n minus 1, divided by 2. Ten teams need 45 matches. It is the fairest format and quickly becomes the longest.

A Swiss-system tournament pairs contestants with similar running scores without repeating opponents. Wikipedia says the number of rounds is fixed in advance, that it suits events with too many entrants for a full round-robin but where you do not want to eliminate anyone early, and that organizers usually rely on a computer program for the pairings. A tie-break such as the sum of opponents' scores, known as Buchholz, decides ties.

sections.h2: Match the format to your event
paras: Use this as a first filter, then adjust for your game's match length.
list: Short window, large field, lowest stakes: single elimination, accepting the variance.
Competitive field where a single upset should not decide everything: double elimination, with a power-of-two field to avoid byes.
Small field, longer window, league feel: round-robin, possibly followed by a playoff for the top few.
Large field, want everyone to keep playing: Swiss for a fixed number of rounds, then a single-elimination top cut.
Unknown signup count: build a group stage that scales, and set a cap and a waitlist in advance.

sections.h2: Write the rules before opening registration
paras: The rules are the real product of an online event. Players will read them when something goes wrong, so they have to answer the likely questions in plain words. Cover eligibility, roster changes, the game version and settings, map or character pick and ban procedure, and scheduling windows.

Online play adds its own gaps, because you cannot see the room. Define what counts as a disconnect and how many are allowed. State who can pause and for how long. Say how results are reported and who confirms them, and what evidence is needed, such as a screenshot of the final scoreboard or a replay file. Write the penalty ladder, from warning to forfeit to disqualification, so that no one is making it up under pressure.

Add integrity language too. The Esports Integrity Commission, ESIC, has described a framework in which tournament organizers adopt ESIC integrity provisions and model clauses in their tournament rules, participation agreements and terms. If your event has prize money or betting exposure, read what ESIC publishes and borrow its clause structure rather than inventing your own.

sections.h2: Pick the platform and set up registration
paras: A tournament platform handles registration, seeding, bracket generation, result reporting and notifications, which is most of the hand work. start.gg, for example, describes itself as a destination to create, run, play and watch esports tournaments, with a Create Tournament flow, rankings and a developer portal. For a comparison of the field, including features for check-in and dispute handling, see [Best Esports Tournament Management Software](/software/best-esports-tournament-management-software).
Whichever you choose, set up the following before opening signups.
list: Create the event with the format, game, start time and time zone stated once, in one place.
Paste the rules in full, not as a link to a document that can change.
Set the registration cap, the close date and the check-in window.
Collect the contact handle you will actually use on match day, such as a Discord username, and the in-game ID.
Decide how seeding works: random, ranked by prior results, or manual.
Test the result-reporting flow with two dummy accounts.
after: Open a community channel for the event. If you use Discord, the moderation setup in [How to Moderate a Discord Server](/guides/how-to-moderate-a-discord-server) applies directly to a tournament server.

paras: No-shows break online brackets more than anything else. Check-in is the tool against them: players confirm they are present before the bracket is locked, and anyone who has not is removed and replaced from the waitlist. Set the check-in window to close long enough before the first match that you can rebuild the bracket without panic.

In Swiss and round-robin formats, a late forfeit also distorts standings, so state in the rules how a forfeited match is scored. For elimination formats, state that a no-show loses by forfeit and the opponent advances after a fixed wait time. Posting that time in the channel at the start of each round avoids a round of messages.

sections.h2: Staff match day with clear roles
paras: A small event can run on a few people if each knows their lane. Give each role a name and a channel, so that players know whom to ask.
list: Head admin: owns rulings and is the only person who can overturn a result.
Match admins: watch one or two matches each, answer questions, record results.
Check-in desk: removes no-shows and adjusts the bracket.
Tech support: handles lobby and connection issues.
Broadcast lead, if you stream: tells admins which matches are on air.
after: Keep a single shared log of rulings. When the same dispute comes up in round three, you want to apply the same answer you gave in round one, and the log shows that you did.

sections.h2: Plan the broadcast if you want one
paras: A stream is optional, and it multiplies the work. Decide early whether you will broadcast only the final, a featured match each round, or everything. Featured matches need admin coordination, because players must be ready on time and observer or spectator slots need to be set up.

If you do broadcast, the scene setup, scoreboard graphics and casting audio are their own project. [Best Esports Broadcast Production Software](/software/best-esports-broadcast-production-software) compares the options, and [How to Set Up Stream Overlays and Alerts](/guides/how-to-set-up-stream-overlays-and-alerts) covers the overlay side. Budget a test match before the event, with the same accounts and settings you will use live.

Publish final standings and results as soon as the last ruling is settled, and keep the bracket page live for a fixed period for reference. If there are prizes, confirm each winner's payment details privately and announce the payout timeline publicly.

Then hold a short review with your admins within a few days, while memories are fresh. Write down which rules caused arguments, which rounds ran late and why, and what you would change. Fold those into the ruleset for the next event, and publish the revised version with a date.

faqs.q: Which bracket format is best for a first online tournament?
faqs.a: For a first event, single elimination or double elimination on a power-of-two field is easiest to explain and schedule. Single elimination needs one fewer match than teams. Double elimination gives each team a second life at the cost of roughly twice the matches. Choose by how many hours you can host, not by what looks most professional.

faqs.q: How many matches does a round-robin need?
faqs.a: Each pair of participants meets once in a single round-robin, so the count is n times n minus 1, divided by 2. Ten teams need 45 matches, and a double round-robin doubles that. This is why round-robins suit small fields or leagues with a longer calendar, and large fields lean to Swiss or elimination.

It is a format where a fixed number of rounds is announced in advance and each round pairs contestants with similar scores, never repeating an opponent. Nobody is eliminated early. It is useful when a full round-robin is too long, and software normally does the pairing because the rules are complicated.

faqs.q: What should online tournament rules cover?
faqs.a: Eligibility, rosters, game version and settings, pick and ban process, schedule windows, check-in, disconnect and pause handling, result reporting with evidence, a penalty ladder and a dispute path. Online events need the last four most, because admins cannot see the room and players cannot settle things face to face.

faqs.q: Do I need an integrity framework for a small community cup?
faqs.a: A small cup without prize money can stay light, but it still benefits from clear anti-cheating, match-fixing and conduct rules. If prizes or betting are involved, look at published frameworks such as ESIC's, which describe adding integrity provisions and model clauses to tournament rules and participation agreements.
